results.title: NVIDIA B200 Price in 2026: Specs and GPU Pricing | fal
results.author: Jim Cai
highlights:
Jim Cai· Updated Oct 19, 2026· 9 min read

The NVIDIA B200 is the first-generation Blackwell data-center GPU: 192 GB HBM3e, 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth, NVLink 5 and native FP4. Few teams buy one outright, so the price that matters is the rental rate. B200 time is sold three ways: an hourly list rate, per-second billing on serverless platforms, and lower reserved or committed rates. On fal Serverless a B200 costs $7.99 per GPU-hour at list price, billed per second only while a runner is alive, and as low as $5.49 per GPU-hour with committed capacity.

...

The B200 is the first data-center GPU in NVIDIA's Blackwell generation. It follows the Hopper-based H100 and H200, and it sits one step below the Blackwell Ultra B300. 1 

Three changes set it apart from Hopper:

- Memory. 192 GB of HBM3e per GPU, up from 141 GB on the H200 and 80 GB on the H100. 2 
- Bandwidth. 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth, about 1.7 times the H200. Most inference is limited by memory bandwidth, so this is the number that moves tokens per second and frames per second. 2 
- FP4. Blackwell adds a native 4-bit floating-point format (NVFP4). Hopper has no FP4 path, so FP4 throughput is new rather than faster. 3

...

### Hourly (on-demand) rates

The headline number is an hourly price per GPU. Two questions decide what you actually pay at that rate:

- What is the smallest unit you can rent? Some offers only rent whole 8-GPU servers, so the real hourly price is eight times the per-GPU rate.
- What is the billing granularity? Hourly billing rounds up. A 10-minute test on an hourly plan costs a full hour.

...

The lowest B200 rates come from a commitment: reserved runners, a spend commitment or a longer contract. You trade flexibility for a lower per-hour price and guaranteed capacity. Reserved pricing makes the most sense when your baseline traffic keeps GPUs busy around the clock. Many teams combine a reserved baseline with per-second capacity on top for peaks.

## fal's B200 price

Prices as of October 19, 2026, taken from fal.ai/pricing. 7 Check that page for the current rate before you plan a budget.

| GPU | VRAM | List price | As low as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 192 GB | $7.99/h | $5.49/h |

The list price is the per-GPU hourly rate, billed per second while a runner is alive. The "as low as" rate depends on your capacity arrangement, such as reserved runners or a usage commitment. Contact sales for those terms.

At the list price, one B200 second costs about $0.00222. Some worked examples:

| Workload | Billed GPU time | Cost at list price | Cost at "as low as" |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10-minute test run on 1 GPU | 600 GPU-seconds | $1.33 | $0.92 |
| 1 hour on an 8-GPU runner | 8 GPU-hours | $63.92 | $43.92 |
| 1 GPU kept warm for a 30-day month | 720 GPU-hours | $5,752.80 | $3,952.80 |
| Bursty traffic: 3 runner-hours a day, 30 days | 90 GPU-hours | $719.10 | $494.10 |

The last two rows show why scaling to zero matters as much as the hourly rate. The same B200 costs one-eighth as much per month when it runs only while traffic needs it.

### B200 or H200 on price

Most inference is limited by memory bandwidth, so the hourly price per TB/s of bandwidth is a rough guide to cost per output. Using fal's published rates: 5 7 

| GPU | Memory bandwidth | List price | List price per TB/s | As low as | As low as per TB/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 8 TB/s | $7.99/h | $1.00 | $5.49/h | $0.69 |
| H200 | 4.8 TB/s | $6.00/h | $1.25 | $2.99/h | $0.62 |
| H100 | 3.35 TB/s | $4.50/h | $1.34 | $2.49/h | $0.74 |

At list prices the B200 is the cheapest of the three per unit of bandwidth. At the lowest committed rates the H200 is slightly cheaper, so if you are committing to capacity for a model that fits in 141 GB, benchmark both before you choose.

...

### How much does an NVIDIA B200 cost?

NVIDIA does not publish a list price for the B200, and it is mostly sold inside 8-GPU servers, so for most teams the useful number is the rental rate. On fal Serverless a B200 costs $7.99 per GPU-hour at list price, billed per second, and as low as $5.49 per GPU-hour with reserved capacity or a usage commitment. These rates are as of October 19, 2026; current rates are on fal.ai/pricing.

results.author: Jim Cai
highlights:
| Criterion | What to ask | How fal answers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold start | How long from "no warm runner" to first response, for a model my size? What shortens it? | Weights load with FlashPack, fal's open-source loader, at about 3.1 GB/s: a 20 GB model's weights land in six to seven seconds. Keep warm runners with `min_concurrency` so requests skip the cold start.

...

| SLA | What uptime is contractually committed? | 99.99% uptime SLA. |
| GPU capacity | Will a GPU be free when my traffic spikes? How long do requests wait for hardware at peak, and is that wait billed? | Thousands of GPUs, running every model on fal for three years. List more than one machine type and fal falls back to the next when the first has no capacity. Time spent waiting for hardware is not billed. |
| Billing granularity | Per second, per minute or per hour? Which states are billed: setup, idle, image pull, failed requests? | Per second, for the time runners are alive. Image pulls and pending time are not billed. 5xx errors are not charged. |
| GPU types and price | Which GPUs can I get on demand, with how much memory, at what rate? | B300, GB200, B200, H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000, from $4.00 to $12.99 per GPU-hour (table below). |
| Max concurrency | Is there an account-level cap on my own endpoints? Who controls it? | You set `max_concurrency`. Account concurrency limits do not apply when you call your own Serverless endpoints. |
| Scale-to-zero | Does it scale to zero by default? How long do idle runners stay up, and is that time billed? | Yes. `min_concurrency` defaults to 0. Idle runners stay up for `keep_alive` (default 60 s), and that idle time is billed. |
| Container support | Can I bring a Dockerfile? A pre-built image from a private registry? | A Dockerfile, or a pre-built image from any registry, including private ones. |
| Observability | Logs, traces, metrics, alerts? Can I export them to my own stack? | Logs, request traces, analytics and latency breakdowns in one dashboard. Alerts in the app, in Slack and by email. A Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint and log drains. |
| Migration effort | Do I rewrite my server, or wrap it? Is there a guide for my setup? | An existing Docker server can run with zero code changes: fal starts your container and routes requests to its port. Python inference servers can be wrapped in a `fal.App`. See the migration guides. |

...

### GPU types and price

Match memory to your model first, then match speed to your latency target. A model that does not fit in one GPU's memory needs a multi-GPU runner, and every GPU in it is billed for the whole time the runner is alive:

Runner cost per hour = number of GPUs × per-GPU hourly rate

For example, a model that needs 120 GB of GPU memory does not fit on one H100 (80 GB). On two H100s it costs 2 × $4.50 = $9.00 per hour. On one H200 (141 GB) it costs $6.00 per hour, a third less, even though the H200 has the higher hourly rate. So price the smallest set of GPUs your model fits on, not the cheapest GPU.

fal's published serverless rates on October 19, 2026:

| GPU | Memory | Per GPU-hour | Per second (approx.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 | 288 GB | $12.99 | $0.00361 |
| GB200 | 192 GB | $9.99 | $0.00278 |
| B200 | 192 GB | $7.99 | $0.00222 |
| H200 | 141 GB | $6.00 | $0.00167 |
| H100 | 80 GB | $4.50 | $0.00125 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 96 GB | $4.00 | $0.00111 |

Check fal.ai/pricing for current rates. Newer GPUs cost more per hour but can finish each request faster, so compare cost per request, not cost per hour:

Cost per request = hourly rate ÷ 3,600 × billed seconds per request ÷ requests served at once per runner.

Multiplexing and idle time move this more than list price. For one GPU in depth, see NVIDIA B200 Price in 2026.

results.title: Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal
highlights:
# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

results.author: Paul Nugent
highlights:
# AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at

Paul Nugent

Nov 4, 2026

AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

This is the most important AI infrastructure pricing story of the year, and the signal is unmistakable.

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

The critical detail: Trainium pricing is unchanged.

AWS now operates two parallel compute economics tracks:

🔹 NVIDIA TRACK: +20% — you absorb Nvidia's pricing power, supply constraints, AND AWS's margin protection layered on top.

🔹 TRAINIUM TRACK: flat — Amazon subsidizes the economics because every workload that migrates to Trainium deepens lock-in to the AWS ecosystem.
